study_identification_part.si4_title: Dissecting task-based fMRI activity using normative modelling: an application to the Emotional Face Matching Task

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study demonstrates the application of normative modelling to task-based fMRI data to characterize individual differences in functional activity evoked by the Emotional Face Matching Task (EFMT). The aim is to estimate large-scale normative models that bind heterogeneous datasets to a common reference, dissect heterogeneity underlying group-level analyses, and map individual differences in patients with mental health diagnoses relative to the reference cohort.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Data pre-processing was harmonised across all sites; a FSL-based pipeline was consistently applied to decrease the likelihood of introducing variance due to pre-processing differences... At a within-subject level, all functional data underwent gradient unwarping, motion correction, fieldmap-based EPI distortion correction (where fieldmaps were available), boundary-based registration of EPI to structural T1-weighted scan, denoising for secondary head motion-related artifacts using automatic noise selection, as implemented in ICA-AROMA, non-linear registration into MNI152 space, and grand-mean intensity normalization. Where applicable, datasets were resampled to 2mm3 resolution, and all data were spatially smoothed using a 5mm FWHM Gaussian kernel.

rci9_quality_checking_detail.answer: Motion exclusion: mean relative RMS >0.5mm (17 excluded from DNS, 4 from MIND-Set). Signal coverage QC for UK Biobank: participants ranked by vmPFC coverage and top 5000 selected. Binary ROI masks for dorsal vmPFC, ventral vmPFC, lateral vmPFC, and dorsomedial PFC (Harvard Oxford Atlas 25% probability) used to assess percentage of voxels with signal. Test-retest reliability analysis conducted with HCP Retest data (n=42) to validate deviation score reliability.
rci9_quality_checking_detail.reason: Detailed quality control metrics are provided in the main text and supplementary materials, including specific exclusion criteria, numbers of excluded participants, and methods for assessing signal coverage in problematic regions.
rci9_quality_checking_detail.supporting_text: Participants were excluded if their mean relative RMS was greater than 0.5 mm... Due to air-tissue inhomogeneities which can diminish the acquired BOLD signal to such a degree that no activations are visible, a notorious effect within the ventral PFC, we performed targeted quality control for this extended region. Binary ROI masks were created for the dorsal ventro-medial PFC (d-vmPFC), ventral vmPFC (v-vmPFC), lateral vmPFC (l-vmPFC) and the dorso-medial PFC (dmPFC), as defined by the Harvard Oxford Atlas at 25% probability... We ranked participants in descending order of the percent of their v-vmPFC, l-vmPFC, d-vmPFC, and dmPFC covered, respectively, and selected the first 5000 participants.

rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site included as dummy-coded covariate in Bayesian Linear Regression model. The normative modelling framework binds heterogeneous datasets to a common reference model, which removes site effects from the data without requiring traditional harmonization methods. Acquisition parameters (TR, multiband sequence, number of volumes) and task parameters (task length, number of target blocks, instructions, target stimuli) were also included as covariates, some of which are collinear with site. Structure coefficients were used to interpret effects due to collinearity among predictor variables.
rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper clearly describes the model-based approach to handling site effects through covariate inclusion in the normative model, and explicitly discusses how this approach differs from traditional harmonization methods. The paper also notes the benefits of this approach.
rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: A key feature of the normative modelling framework in the context of multi-site fMRI data is that it allows us to aggregate data across multiple samples by binding them to a common reference model. This provides multiple benefits: it removes site effects from the data without requiring the data to be harmonized, which avoids the introduction of certain biases due to harmonisation and allows meaningful comparisons to be drawn across studies... We included dummy coded site-related variables as additional covariates of no-interest... Some input variables, namely acquisition parameters, showed overlapping effects (with sensical direction flips) likely due to their relatively high correlation and limited variability across sites

nm8_nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study handles several sources of nuisance structure: (1) Site effects are modeled as covariates; (2) Acquisition parameters (TR, multiband, volumes) are included; (3) Motion artifacts are addressed through ICA-AROMA denoising and exclusion criteria; (4) Signal dropout in vmPFC is acknowledged and QC performed; (5) Age is modeled linearly. However, the study does not explicitly model heteroscedasticity (though BLR provides prediction variance), does not use hierarchical/random effects for site, and does not explicitly address within-site or within-subject correlation structures. The paper notes collinearity among predictors but uses structure coefficients for interpretation rather than addressing it directly in the model.
nm8_nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: We created normative models of EFMT-related BOLD activation maps, as a function of site, age, sex, intra-cranial volume, and acquisition [TR, multiband sequence, number of volumes collected]... Data pre-processing... denoising for secondary head motion-related artifacts using automatic noise selection, as implemented in ICA-AROMA... Participants were excluded if their mean relative RMS was greater than 0.5 mm... In our sample many predictor variables were collinear across sites which limited our ability to detect systematic differences... we decided to keep all variables in the model and used structure coefficients to identify the importance of different variables, which are relatively insensitive to collinearity.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (Normative Probability Maps, NPM), thresholded at |Z| > 2.6 (p < .005). Deviation scores represent the difference between predicted and true activation scaled by prediction variance. Frequency of extreme deviations counted per participant. Unthresholded deviation maps used for SCCA analyses.

The subject-specific Z-score indicates the difference between the predicted activation and true activation scaled by the prediction variance. We thresholded participant's NPM at Z = ± 2.6 (i.e. p < .005)... we compared the frequency of extreme deviations (NPMs thesholded at > ± 2.6), at the level of each individual... we input whole-brain deviation maps (unthresholded, such that any deviations, irrespective of their magnitude, could potentially contribute to the observed correlations)

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis (SCCA) with L1-norm regularization to relate whole-brain unthresholded deviation maps to transdiagnostic functional domain scores (negative valence, cognitive function, social processes, arousal/inhibition). Used 70-30 train-test split with 10-fold cross-validation. Statistical significance assessed via 1000-fold permutation testing. Regularization parameters set heuristically (c1=0.9√p for factor scores, c2=0.1√q for deviation maps). Mann-Whitney U tests compared frequency of deviations between patients and reference cohort. Separate SCCA attempted for diagnostic labels vs deviations (not significant).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Considerable inter-individual variation in task-evoked fMRI activation underlies group effects; deviation patterns from faces>shapes models showed higher frequency in patients and associated with negative valence/arousal domains; deviation patterns from faces>baseline models showed stronger associations with cognitive functioning and arousal/inhibition domains; no significant association between diagnostic labels and deviations.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Normative models achieved good explained variance (up to 0.525) in test set, particularly in visual cortex and amygdala. Inter-individual variability was substantial, with every voxel showing at least one subject with extreme deviation (|Z|>2.6), most frequently in medial occipital lobe, fusiform gyrus, and inferior temporal lobe. Deviation scores showed moderate-to-good test-retest reliability (ICC), with 94.8% of voxels showing no significant differences between sessions. Structure coefficients revealed interpretable effects: age related to decreased peripheral activation and increased DMN activation; sex (female) related to increased insula/cingulate activation; task design (matching expression vs. faces) and stimuli type (Ekman vs. Nim-Stim) showed distinct activation patterns. Traditional case-control comparison found minimal differences between patients and controls. However, patients showed significantly higher frequency of deviations for faces>shapes (Mann-Whitney U=341806.5, p=2.029×10⁻⁵) but not for faces>baseline (U=487921.0, p=0.22). SCCA revealed significant out-of-sample associations between deviations and transdiagnostic symptom domains: faces>shapes deviations (mean r=0.224, p<0.001) associated with negative valence/arousal involving insula, mPFC, hippocampus, thalamus; faces>baseline deviations (mean r=0.180, p<0.001) associated with cognitive function/arousal involving bilateral insula, ACC, caudate, putamen, amygdala. No significant association between diagnostic labels and deviations (r<0.1). Spatial heterogeneity analysis showed highly variable deviation patterns both within and across diagnostic categories, with only ~20% of patients showing extreme deviations in any given voxel.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The normative modelling framework demonstrates utility for binding heterogeneous multi-site fMRI datasets to a common reference without traditional harmonization, avoiding potential harmonization-induced biases. The approach allows for meaningful individual-level comparisons across studies and enables parsing of heterogeneity. The study demonstrates that approaching dysfunction through normative modelling and transdiagnostic functional domains may more closely relate to underlying biology than traditional diagnostic categories. The method can be extended to other fMRI tasks and could be used to predict various outcomes beyond functional activation. Authors encourage applying this approach to other neuroimaging tasks. Future work could incorporate test-retest variability directly into models to provide lower bounds on meaningful deviation magnitude, or use hierarchical models to accommodate within-subject dependencies when multiple scans are available. Clustering algorithms could be applied to derive subject stratifications, and supervised learning methods could assess prediction of specific clinical variables from deviation patterns.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Participants in mid-adulthood (ages 37-46) were under-represented, potentially limiting generalizability across the full lifespan. Collinearity among predictor variables (particularly site-related variables and acquisition/task parameters) limited ability to fully separate effects, though structure coefficients were used to address this. Signal dropout in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (particularly for UK Biobank) affected deviation score reliability in this region, requiring cautious interpretation. Explained variance was low for the clinical cohort, as expected due to homogeneity in acquisition parameters and narrow age range. Test-retest reliability, while generally good, varied by region. Clinical sample had high diagnostic co-morbidity, which both reflects naturalistic populations but also complicates diagnosis-specific interpretations. The study notes general concerns about within-subject reliability of task-based fMRI, though their test-retest analysis provides some reassurance.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is the first large-scale application of normative modelling to task-based fMRI, specifically the Emotional Face Matching Task. The study included 6 independent sites with varying scanner types (3T Siemens Skyra, Prisma, Magentom Prisma; 3T Phillips Achieva dStream; 3T GE MR750), different acquisition parameters (TR: 720-2000ms; TE: 28-39ms; multiband factors: 6-8 where applicable), and task design variations (trial duration: 2-5s; block structure varied). The HCP Retest sample (n=42) was used specifically for test-retest reliability analysis. An additional validation was performed with 5000 new UK Biobank participants not included in original training/test splits. The paper provides comprehensive supplementary materials including quality control metrics for vmPFC coverage, motion parameters by site, evaluation metrics (skew, kurtosis, SMSE), test-retest analysis for both contrasts, and spatial patterns of deviations by diagnostic categories. Code is available on GitHub (https://github.com/predictive-clinical-neuroscience/EFMT_Norm_Models) and data on Zenodo. The MIND-Set study was approved by Commissie Mensgebonden Onderzoek Arnhem-Nijmegen. For the MIND-Set cohort, factor loadings for transdiagnostic domains were available for 217 of 236 patients. The study emphasizes moving beyond average brain approaches to understanding individual differences and heterogeneity within clinical populations.
